utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning to you, sir. The affirmation you made still applies. I would mention that Judge Van den Wyngaert is unable to sit today. As we're not sitting tomorrow, I think we can be confident that she will have recovered by the time we sit again next week. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Two brief procedural matters, if I may. Yesterday, Your Honours, at pages 10813 to 10815 of the transcript, the witness and I discussed what was 65 ter 700 of the Prosecution, and my learned colleagues have kindly explained to me, as Ms. Residovic did yesterday as well, that that is actually Exhibit 1D00177. So I just wanted to make sure that the record is clear about that. The second matter, Your Honour, is a request. I've had a discussion with my colleague from the Defence, and both Mr. Tarculovski, of course, and myself have been working hard to make sure that the witness -- excuse me, I made a mistake. I'm not sure where I got that mistake from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think there is a little disease running around the courtroom; it strikes unexpectedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I should have said that I had a conversation with Mr. Apostolski, and both he and I have been working hard to streamline the rest of our questions so that this witness can finish today. The request is simply this. Rather than taking the usual half an hour breaks, we wonder if it would be possible if the two breaks could be shortened to 20 minutes, and that way I will take two sessions to finish my cross-examination with the witness, but that should give my colleague Mr. Apostolski an extra 20 minutes for his redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In some earlier trials, we maintained a 20-minute schedule. But under great pressure from people who found that inadequate for all their purposes, we have changed to half-hour. I'm sure that there will be a willingness of the people who support us, to cooperate just today in managing two 20 minute breaks, rather than half-hour breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Markovski.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On Monday, at page 10633 of the transcript, my colleague asked you: "Did the terrorist group of the NLA have any military structure?" And you responded to that, and at the end of your response, you said the following: "But the so-called brigades worked according to their own independent plans and intentions, and, obviously, this does not speak of an organised structure, let alone an army." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I remember and I confirm this statement today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the man known as Xhavid Asani, he was a member of the NLA's 114th Brigade. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the person that we are discussing; but whether he was precisely in this brigade, I was not able to find a document about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I would refer you to testimony that is at page 5589 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can take a look at your report again, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn, please, to paragraph 371.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 371.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 371 is part of the section of your report 7.4.1, which is titled: Preparations for the operation. And if you take a look at paragraph 371, it starts with a paragraph talking about the organisation and execution of the action by the security forces. Then below that paragraph, we see a series of subparagraphs with some little arrows. Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn to the very last little arrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For those following along in English, in my version at least, it is on page 118. I could be off by a page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The very last little arrow begins with the phrase: "According to information ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are discussing the weekend settlement Basinec, because the Macedonian version does not start with this particular word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, in English version the last little arrow says: "According to information from the diary of events of the 3rd Guardist Battalion." It's a few arrows down the page from the subparagraph that talks about Basinec. Do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the last page before paragraph 372. Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. This little subparagraph says the following: "According to information from the diary of events of the 3rd Guardist Battalion, received at 1520 hours on 11 August 2001, Gzim Ostreni ordered Xhavid Asani to carry out an attack on Rastak and Ljubanci." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as authority for that, you rely on footnote 245, which is the military diary of the 3rd Guards Battalion, which is actually Exhibit 1D00085. Now, could you turn to paragraph 379, please. Paragraph 379, at the start, it talks about documents from the Ministry of Defence "show that its intelligence service possessed valid information on a possible attack by the armed Albanian extremists on the positions of the security forces around Rastak and Ljubanci." Then you give a description of some of this information. Then in the last sentence of the paragraph, you say this: "Added to all of this is also the information that Gzim Ostreni ordered Xhavid Asani to carry out an attack on Rastak and Ljubanci?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is so. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then, in footnote 255, as authority for this information, you cite actually to a different document. It's another report from the Ministry of Defence, this time from the sector for security and counter-intelligence, called: Summary of intelligence information. It's dated the 12th of August, 2001, which has 65 ter number 969.7. So, Dr. Markovski, even your report indicates that Gzim Ostreni issued orders to his subordinates in the field. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is right, but, here, it does not say that the Chief of Staff of the NLA issued the order to the commander of, let's say, the 114th Brigade. So the Chief of Staff, Gzim Ostreni, issued an order to the commander of the 114th Brigade - WHAT was his name - the person, as you mentioned him. So we are not discussing here military order in the senses of chain of command. It just says that a person such-and-such gave an order to another person. Why is it not possible in a terrorist organisation for one person to tell another person what to do so. So we have not discussing here a situation of subordinate and superior, nor we are discussing an organised planned manner of commanding or taking action.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, but in your testimony, at page 10633 of the transcript, you said: "But the so-called brigades worked according to their own independent plans and intentions." But we see here that, even in your own report, you indicate that that wasn't necessarily true, was it? We see Gzim Ostreni giving orders to members of the brigades, or to a member of a brigade?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One has to be fully correct. I'm not saying that the brigades operated independently according to their own plans; but, basically, I corroborate or I cite the position of Mr. Gzim Ostreni provided in his own statement. And if one reads well my statement, this position of mine in the report points out to the fact that this was stated by Mr. Gzim Ostreni.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to a slightly different topic, if we can. Can you turn back, please, to paragraph 239 of your report. Dr. Markovski, we looked at this paragraph briefly yesterday, and we -- we looked at the four conditions that you describe at the end of the paragraph, with which -- which should be in place for a unit of a movement of organised resistance to be an armed force. The last condition that you put here is that: "That they adhere to the rules of warfare during combat actions?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, now, one of the international organisations that addresses this kind of issue is the ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were -- it's a structure presence in the Republic of Macedonia during the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness a video-clip, please, and this will be 65 ter 1118.9. It has ERN number VOOO-7472, clip 9. Your Honours, you can find the transcript of this clip at tab 65 in binder 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Markovski, this is video material produced --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If Dr. Markovski needs the third binder, could that be given to him, please. But you should be able to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Hopefully you will be able to hear this, Doctor. And, Doctor, this is video material produced by Macedonia Radio and Television on the 23rd of May, 2001. It's a press conference with members of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we see that video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So we see from this report that there was some contact at that time, May, between members of the ICRC and members of the NLA. Dr. Markovski, in 2001, the ICRC was present in Macedonia at least from May until the signing of the Ohrid Agreement. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely until when, but starting May, yes. And, probably, they were present even afterwards, after the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement. I don't remember precisely; however, they were around during the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this video-clip and the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be exhibit number P000607. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Moving to a slightly different topic. At page 10619 of the transcript, you told the Chamber that the NLA used force of arms to achieve political goals, and you also made the comment that the majority of NLA actions were "terrorism." I want to ask you about the attack on the army convoy at Karpalak on the 8th of August, 2001, when ten soldiers, unfortunately, died. Was that an act of terrorism?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. This was a terrorist act, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, first of all, a state of war was not declared in the Republic of Macedonia; that is to say, there were no combat activities planned organised combat activities. And according to the methodology in which this attack was carried out on the convoy, on the members of the armed forces, they were not in a combat position or position to carry out combat activities. They were just being transported from one city to another. So there was no combat situation; and in this particular case, these terrorists used the opportunity provided by the configuration of the terrain. This is a gorge we are discussing. And from the top of the cliffs from both sides of the gorge, they carried out this terrorist attack. So let me repeat. We are not discussing about a combat situation, combat activities. We are just discussing a transport. And in a situation when there is no state of war, any attack on the bodies or institutions of the state is considered as a terrorist attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's go back to our hypothetical country X, if we can, Doctor, and to the hypothetical classic war or classic armed conflict. In a classic war or classic armed conflict, an ambush is not a violation of the rules of war, is it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a classic war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And just to make sure that the record is clear, my question was: "An ambush is not a violation of the rules of war, is it?" Then you said: "In a classic war, yes." So you were agreeing with me. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I did agree with you, because there is one of the methods of the classic type of war, the methods of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, please, if we could bring it up on the screen, what is Exhibit P000467 again, which is the map of the Republic of Macedonia. And if we could zoom in a bit on the upper part of the map, the area from -- yes, that would be good. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, I'm wondering, perhaps with the usher's assistance if you take up the magic pen again, and I'd like to talk to you a limited about where the NLA was operating by the 12th of August, 2001. First of all, by that time, by early/mid-August, there was fighting between the NLA and members of the security forces in and around Tetovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not combat activities. There were armed incidents and provocations by the armed extremist groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fighting is a serious word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, but there was a presence of the NLA in Tetovo. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presence in Tetovo, you mean? No. In the city of Tetovo, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about around Tetovo, in the environs of Tetovo?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the villages around Tetovo, there was fighting in some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you do us a favour? Could you draw a line indicating the villages and the areas where there was a NLA presence and fighting at that time in the Tetovo region.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I might make a mistake; but if you point out a village, then maybe I can respond whether there was something in that particular village or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, I can mention that there was something going on in Sipkovica. But I believe that would be a more efficient method if you point out a village, and then I can confirm it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, let start with the villages that we can see there. Sipkovica, there was fighting in that area, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were not combat activities in Sipkovica. There was an armed group there, and they were acting from there or attacking Tetovo and the surrounding areas. So there was just an armed group in Sipkovica acting or firing in these directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then, let's do this. You say that they were acting from Sipkovica, attacking Tetovo and the surrounding areas. Would you please draw a line, or lines, indicating the areas that were under attack.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, remind me or point out, and then I will tell you yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you see --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are we discussing or what type of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I told you before we're talking about August 2001 up until the 12th of August. Now you're here as an expert on the political/military situation at that time. So I'd like you, please, to help us understand. If you could please indicate on this map the areas where - let's just start with the Tetovo area - where the NLA or members of this armed group were attacking.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you're asking something from me, something that I cannot really afford doing. I can only draw according to my recollections. If it is somewhere to be found in my report, then remind me, and I can explain it further. So if you point out a particular location, I can agree or not, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In Tetovo --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- yes. I understood that we are discussing the area around Tetovo, but, please, can you be more specific? What day, what kind of situation, and what was the side where they were acting from, I can do that; but just to write by heart, I cannot really afford that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you draw a line along the western and north-western side of Tetovo. Can you do that for us?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, this is something that I can do. And north-west, you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And there were armed groups also in - I don't think I'm pronouncing this word correctly - Tearce, the village a bit to the north-east?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an armed group in Tearce as well; not all the time, but from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And could you draw, then, a line from Tearce down to Tetovo?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now there's a road - and, actually, let me stick with the northern-most regions for a moment - to the north of Tearce, going towards Vratnica, there was also the armed groups, wasn't there, or an armed group that had a presence up there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was there Vratnica, especially during the month in August -- actually, just during the month of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can you draw, then, a line up towards Vratnica, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I don't understand the point of this, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there's a road that goes from Tetovo to Gostivar, right? We can see that on the map?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, there was a presence of armed groups in the villages along -- in some of the villages along there road in August 2001, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the villages, if we are talking about to the north of the axillary road, then yes. There was, for instance, in the village of Golema Recica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you draw, then, a line from Golema Recica towards Tetovo.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there was also a presence of armed groups in the area of Bogovinje, wasn't there, by August 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From time to time, there were in Bogovinje as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you draw a line from Bogovinje up to Golema Recica, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, correct me if I'm wrong, there was also the presence of armed groups in the villages of Vrapciste and Negotino, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were in Vrapciste and in Negotino, as well, in the sense that you are asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you draw, then, a line connecting Vrapciste with Negotino, and Negotino with Bogovinje?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, in Gostivar, itself, was there a presence of armed groups?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. In Gostivar, there was no presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about in the -- in the area to the west of Gostivar? Around Vrutok, going towards Debar, there were some presence of armed groups there, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was presentation there. There were no fighting there, apart from one of the places. I hope you will remind me of the name, or was it Tanusevci. It was there only that there was a single exchange of fire during the crisis in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall what month that was?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was after the incident when an anti-tank mine was stepped on by the OSCE representatives. They were killed then and it was immediately after that, but I don't remember the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. That's fine. Now, if we can move, please, from Tetovo now more towards the east. We see the road going from Tetovo through Grupcin and to Skopje. The other day we talked about the presence of armed groups on different sides of that road, to the north and to the south. There was a presence of armed groups, for example, by August around Semsevo, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were there, around Semsevo, in August, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you draw a line from Semsevo down to that road, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And a bit further to the north, in Jegunovce, there was also the presence of an armed group, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I suppose so, because it belongs to the region. Yes, yes. So my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you draw a red line connecting Jegunovce with Semsevo.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, focussing to the south of that road between Tetovo and Skopje, in the area of the Suva Gora mountains, you told us the other day there was an armed group to the south of that road. Can you indicate, approximately, where they were. Was it around Celopek? Was it around Sedlarevo?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will mark it here somewhere roughly. Perhaps it should have been a bit further to the north, but it was somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just for the record, the witness has drawn a red dot a bit to the east of the town of Celopek.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if could you, please, could you draw a line from that red dot up towards the road now.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see the town of Grupcin in the middle of that road between Skopje and Tetovo. By August 2001, the -- there were some armed groups who were carrying out some activities around Grupcin. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, those were the same groups that were located in the northern part, and they were hiding behind or amongst the population in Dvorista and in the southern part in Grupcin. With regards to Grupcin, they couldn't have been there, because the security structures of the army of the Republic of Macedonia and of the police were here. So they could only move from Bojane to Grupcin, or from Dvorista to Grupcin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: In line 15:18, "Bojane" instead of "Grupcin."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We don't see Bojane. Can you indicate on the map approximately where Bojane is?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the dot that I made here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Next to Celopek?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the east of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it should have been a bit further to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And just to keep this clear, could you draw the number 1 next to that red dot, indicating Bojane?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, if we move a bit further east towards Skopje, according to your testimony and I believe your report, by the 12th of August, there was a -- there was presence of an armed group again in Aracinovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was presence in Aracinovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you just draw a circle around Aracinovo, around where it says that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And according to your report and your testimony, there was also armed groups in the village of Ljuboten. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you draw a circle around Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there was a presence of armed groups in Nikustak and Lipkovo. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you draw circles around those villages.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There was a presence of armed groups in the Vaksince area, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in August, no, not in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And in respect to the Kumanovo area, the armed groups got at least as close as Lopate and Romanovce, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They haven't reached Lopate. They couldn't be there. They couldn't have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Romanovce?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither in Romanovce.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: By August of 2001, there was a presence of armed groups in Debar, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no documents with regards to Debar. I have no information that they have been there and that they have acted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Before I forget, can we freeze this image and can this be given an exhibit number, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P00608. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I believe it was also your evidence that some members of the so-called NLA had actually infiltrated Skopje by early August 2001. That was the man known as Commander Teli who died on the 5th of August. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The group of seven or eight members of the person you mentioned and his closest associates has infiltrated Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can leave this map for a moment, if can you just sort of recall where we see the presence of these armed groups now by the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now can we turn now, please, to whether is Exhibit P487, please. Your Honours, this is at tab 88 in binder 3. You've seen it before. It is the map and plan that was produced by Mr. Gzim Ostreni. I don't know whether there's a problem with e-court. We see -- here it comes. Thank you. Can we perhaps focus in on the upper half of this map, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is the map that you discussed a bit during your direct examination, Dr. Markovski; the plan, the map. And during your direct examination on Monday, at page 10646 of the transcript, when discussing this plan, you said that if a commander came to you to take an exam with this kind of plan, you would send him back to first grade to study both tactics and organisation of military structures. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you said that everything written on the original plan is unrealistic and impossible to implement; and then on page 10647 of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Excuse me. I didn't say that everything in the plan was unrealistic. What I said was that unrealistic was the narrative text accompanying the map, in terms of the purposes, the goals that were set, and in terms of achieving those goals. So we were discussing the narrative part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you said, at page 10647 of the transcript, from the military view, this is amateur stuff. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I confirm it again now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. But think back to the positions of the armed groups, or of the NLA, that you drew on a map just a few minutes ago, where they were by August 12, 2001. When we see the positions of the NLA or of these armed groups by 12 August 2001, the plan looks to be pretty successful, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're asking me, specifically. If I understood you well, I agree with the notion that to the north of the axillary road, from Tetovo to the border crossing point Jezince, in the villages populated by ethnic Albanians, the ones that we have mentioned, in those, there were armed extremists, Albanian groups. So from this aspect, I can accept the drawing here. However, one could not accept that, as far as I understood, everything that is marked in yellow here was allegedly under the control of the so-called NLA. First of all, the border-line with the then-Yugoslavia, and later Serbia and Montenegro in the area towards Kosovo, was secured by the Macedonian army. It was both before the crisis and during the crisis in this territory. Because of the inability to efficiently secure the border, we discussed already that the president and other structures in the Republic of Macedonia have requested that KFOR makes special efforts with regards to securing the border from their side. But pursuant to the international standards, the border -- or between the border and the interior of the country, there are two zones. They are called the border belt and the border region. To make it more clear to you, this is actually an identification of the internationally recognised grey and green zone, or the green zone is the in depth territory 100 metres from the border-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, please. I am explaining the map. I wish to explain where the armed groups were and where they controlled the territory, because this is the specific question you asked me. Will you allow me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, that's not the specific question that I asked you. The question I asked you was that: When you look at where the armed groups were by the 12th of August, 2001, when you look at this plan for where the armed groups were supposed to be during the summer of 2001, then the plan actually looks fairly -- the results of the plan actually look to be fairly successful, because we see the plan of the NLA presence around Tetovo, that's the green arrows; we see the NLA moving towards Skopje; we see the armed groups moving to the north of the road between Tetovo and Skopje and coming as well towards that road from the south. So wouldn't it be fair to say that a large portion of this plan was actually realised by the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not like that, Mr. Saxon. This story that you are developing now has nothing to do with this map, and I don't know we are looking at this map. If you wish to corroborate your story with this map, then allow me to finish my explanation and tell you that these armed groups that were in the villages we mentioned and discussed, that is a fact. But this map gives a false image when we looking at it. And the notion that they moved freely and whenever they wanted there is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At page 10634 of the transcript on Monday, in response to a question of my colleague, you said: "I never came across a document which would speak of any planned organised action by these so-called organised brigades."

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I confirm it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn back to your report, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We can remove this map from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn to paragraph 336 of your report. Paragraph 336, it's part of the -- of section 7.2 which is titled: Origin of the events in and around Ljuboten. I would like to review with you paragraphs 336 and 337, if we can. First of all, in paragraph 335, you explain that: "The occurrences in the village of Ljuboten need to be analysed in the context of the overall events of that period in the crisis regions." And then this paragraph 336, you explain where Ljuboten is located, about ten kilometres to the north-east of Skopje; that there are mountains running to the north and north-east of the village; that pack animals can be used or people can go by foot along these mountains; sometimes motor vehicles can be used in certain terrain. Then you describe the different paths that go through these areas around Matejce, monastery, and the villages of Matejce and Nikustak, and the other path beginning at Blace continuing to Skopje and Aracinovo. And then this paragraph 237 [sic], you say the following: "These routes were used extensively at the start of the crisis in the Republic of Macedonia for the relocation of armed groups of Albanian extremists, and for the transport of weapons and other equipment by various criminals and armed Albanian extremists. At the start of June, these routes were used by some 250 armed Albanian extremists to reach the village of Aracinovo. "Their aim," it may be purpose in the original Macedonian, "was to drive out the non-ethnic Albanian population from the villages in the vicinity of Ljuboten and Aracinovo, through terrorist sabotage activities in the wider region of Skopje, and on buildings of vital significant to the daily lives of the population and through intimidation, thus generating ethnic cleansing, while also endeavouring to obtain concessions from the government of the Republic of Macedonia, in order 'to resolve the Albanian issue.'" Have you been following me, with me?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is a really good conclusion that I've made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, assuming that the information in these paragraphs is correct, doesn't the activity that you describe require a certain level of planning and organisation?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So it just happened sort of spontaneously. Is that how it all happened?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it happened spontaneously, but the purpose was something completely different. We do not have here -- I really can't understand what is your view to this? Do you think that a brigade, or let's go down to a level of a battalion, that a battalion would freely and in a planned fashion work and transport the illegal weapons from Kosovo into the Republic of Macedonia, or in whatever other direction, regardless of the difficulties that the terrain in the geographic sense in this area presents. So this could not have be the organised groups doing it. This is done by individuals, two, three, four people, using animals for transport. They can't even use vehicles for transport, and they used the configuration of the terrain. They used the night-time and they use the fog that is also present within a certain period here, because these arms were brought here as early as March. This does not say that we have a planned and organised activity. What we have is certain activities of the armed Albanian extremist groups that do this in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that the record is clear, you say: We have individuals or small groups of people using the configuration of the terrain, the fog, using animals to transport things like weapons, to different villages in the areas to the north of Skopje. And that activity had to be done in that way, because it would have been dangerous to do it any other way, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any time, they did it before the crisis, and then they needed to cover, to hide from the police controls from the police teams that was controlling the area. That was regular activity of the police in the peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So to do all of this activity in difficult terrain, in difficult weather conditions, using animals, doing it in secret, you think this was something that required a fair amount of planning and organisation?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is not the level of organisation of an armed force, and it is not a level of planned activity of an armed structure, such as brigades, that you keep indicating allegedly existed. But I'm telling you that there is no document that any brigade existed, that any General Staff existed. Really, I wish to say publicly, if you prove to me or if give me a document about the existence of any brigade, I will completely step back from this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, what I think that you're explaining to us is that the members of the so-called NLA were actually operating in circumstances that were more difficult than what a classic army would normally face, right? They had to use pack animals, they had to operate in bad weather at night. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that takes a lot of planning and organisation and care, doesn't it, to do that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look here, I'm from a village originally, so when I need to load the donkey with some cargo, I don't need any special organisation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can move on to paragraph 338, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The last sentence of paragraph 338 says that: "While the 1st Guardist Brigade took up these positions, police officers from Cair police station set up check-points on the roads between Ljubanci and Ljuboten and next to the church in Ljuboten in the direction of the village of Rastak." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why was it important at this time, in mid-June, for the police to set up those check-points?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was important because immediately before that, there were direct -- there was direct evidence about smuggling of weapons, transport and warehousing of the weapons in this particular region. For this reason, in order to prevent or terminate the link between Ljuboten with Nikustak, that is to say, with Matejce, and in order to prevent for the village of Ljuboten to be used as logistic support, in any sense, for these armed groups that were to be found there, probably, according to the estimates of the Ministry of Interior, the conclusion was made that it is necessary to establish these check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And in that kind of a security situation, it is also important to keep those check-points manned and keep them reinforced. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A check-point on its own means people. This is not a facility. A check-point means people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So the answer to my question would be yes, then, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you take a look, please, at paragraphs 342 to 343. Paragraph 342 begins with the extraction of the armed Albanian extremists from Aracinovo on the 26th of June, 2001. You say that the majority of them ended up in Nikustak, but then you say: "A smaller number of the armed extremists returned to Ljuboten on foot, through the village of Rastak." You say: "These were the armed extremist groups with Xhavid Asani and Nazmi Sulejmani. Their return to Ljuboten aimed to maintain the tension in the area of Skopska Crna Gora by preparing and undertaking activities to continue the armed provocations, incidents, and terrorist actions against the members and buildings of the Ministry of Interior and the army of the Republic of Macedonia." And then in paragraph 343, you say this: "The village of Ljuboten became a logistics base for the area of Skopje for the armed extremists groups in the Kumanovo-Lipkovo region. Weapons, military equipment, and sanitary material from Skopje were transported to Ljuboten and then onto the Kumanovo-Lipkovo region over the mountains in the Skopje Crna Gora with domestic pack animals." Again, assuming that the information in these paragraphs is correct, doesn't this activity, the establishment of a logistics base for the area of Skopje in the village of Ljuboten, doesn't that require a certain level of planning and organisation?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really refrain all the time to make a comparison, but now I would like to apologise to the Macedonian public, and I have to say that Al Qaeda does the same things that you are discussing now. But nobody, nor you or I, did not represent them as an armed force, but we talked about them as terrorists. Your thesis that this is a planned activity conducted by an organised military structure, indeed, does not hold water.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To finish up on this topic, and, of course, since 2001, the government and military of the United States of America has been at war with Al Qaeda, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know - now I have to apologise to the American public, because I'm going to mention a tragic event, 11th of September, 2001, and probably we all remember it well - the President Bush declared a war to the organised terrorist and declared war to global terrorism. I'm not quite sure that the United States are really in war with global terrorism; however, they are part of an anti-terrorist coalition, and together with me own country as well we are trying to resolve a registrar serious probably in Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Moving to a different topic, can we turn please to paragraph 369. This is at the start of section 7.4, called: The operation by the security forces on 12 August 2001. Then 369 comes under the subheading: Preparations for the operation. In this paragraph, you say, according to your analysis of the documents, "the operation of the security forces of 12 August 2001 was prepared on the idea and verbal order of the president of the Republic of Macedonia, Boris Trajkovski." Then you say: "He was under intense pressure for an extended period, both from the Macedonian public and certain political circles, and it is possible that he decided on this course of action in order to prevent the further escalation of the crisis in the Skopje region, while also taking into account the seriousness of potential terrorist acts and the pressure of the armed Albanian extremists on the non-ethnic Albanian population to leave the villages around Skopje?" First of all, you use the phrase "it is possible" in this sentence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring about the seriousness of possible terrorist attacks, the answer is yes, because this is an assumption, a possible threat as a danger is possible. They haven't happened but they are possible. If we would like to act preventively, then we have to make serious assessment. And, in doing so, we have to point out possible threats in any of the segments of security or any part of the territory of the Republic of Macedonia; and, accordingly, in the preventative sense, we have to prepare and prevent this kind of incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, I'm going to stop you. Perhaps my question wasn't clear. In the second sentence of this paragraph, referring to President Trajkovski, you say: "He was under intense pressure for an extended period, both from the Macedonian public and certain political circles, and it is possible that he decided on this course of action," et cetera, et cetera. You use the term "it is possible" because this sentence is conjecture on your part; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The probably here is the translation again. I apologise. Maybe that is why my previous anticipate was regarding the possibilities because this sentence speaks about the possibility. In the original text, I'm talking about a fully realistic assessment and not possible. So this is an error in the translation. I'm not talking about a possibility but a realistic assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Markovski, just to speed this up, could you simply read in your language the second sentence of paragraph 369, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. "During a longer period, the president of the Republic of Macedonia was under an intense pressure, both by the Macedonian public and also certain political circles, and the assessment is completely realistic that he decided to do so in order to prevent further escalation of the crisis in the Skopje region, at the same time having in mind the seriousness of possible terrorist acts and the pressure by the armed Albanian extremists on the non-Albanian population to move out from the villages in the area surrounding Skopje."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the phrase, though, "and the assessment is completely realistic." That is still your conjecture, isn't it? You don't know that to be a fact, do you, why the president did what he did?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I draw this conclusion. I don't know precisely what the president was thinking, what he undertook, and what he was going to undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And looking at the last part of that sentence -- well, no, let's look at the sentence on the whole. It is a long sentence. But you think, or you suggest, that the president decided on this course of action "to prevent further escalation of the crisis in the Skopje region." Then you also say that he had in mind or might have had in mind "the seriousness of possible terrorist act and the pressure by the armed Albanian extremists on the non-Albanian population." So I'm just trying to understand, if the president wanted to prevent the further escalation of the crisis in the Skopje region, why, then, would he order an operation, a military operation, on an ethnic Albanian village close to Skopje? Why would he do that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, he did not order an action against the population of the Albanian ethnicity in the Skopje region. He had in mind all the information that he received, and during the previous few days, the information about the movement of armed groups, for instance, the penetration in Aracinovo of such an armed group, then the movement in and around the village of Ljuboten. And, of course, by accepting the recommendations of his professional associates in the defence area who were capable of pointing out that the purpose of this movement in and around the village of Ljuboten, actually it is the creation of a compact territory from the Kumanovo region towards to the mountain of Zeden, because the only problem related to any further movement of the armed groups is precisely this area, because also they're not linked, and the possibility to penetrate from the territory in Kosovo. So the president, on the basis of all the aforementioned, he could have drawn this kind of conclusion. His purpose was not attack on Ljuboten, but preventing any further movement in order to establish some kind of contact territory, and in order to prevent any infiltration of these groups in the city of Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. At the end of paragraph 369 -- well, first of all, in the remainder of paragraph 369, you talk about how the preparations for the action were conducted in secret and only in the circle of those that would be its direct perpetrators: The 3rd Battalion of the 1st Guardist Brigade and the Cair internal affairs department. You say: "This was, nevertheless, logical. It must be taken into account that the chief of the General Staff was changed on 10 August 2001. A new one had not been appointed, and the preparations demanded a certain degree of planning."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is 65 ter 971. That's the document that Dr. Markovski cites to in footnote 228. This is not in your binder, Your Honour, but we'll look at it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a statement, Doctor, provided by General Metodija Stamboliski to the Office of the Prosecutor, I believe in late -- I believe it was December 2003. General Stamboliski says the following about 12 August 2001: "At around 0830 hours in the capacity of deputy chief of the army of the Republic of Macedonia General Staff, and at the same time as the acting chief of the army of Republic of Macedonia General Staff (pursuant to the decree dated 10 August 2001 and issued by the president of the Republic of Macedonia, General Pande Petrovski was relieved of his duties and no replacement was appointed and, therefore, he continued to be present in the cabinet of the chief of General Staff), I set off from my office to see General Pande Petrovski, on which occasion we both heard that there had been firing and detonations coming from the direction of Skopska Crna Gora at that time?" Then later on, General Stamboliski says he went to find General Sokol Mitrevski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He's just got to his feet. I was waiting for you to finish. Yes. We will turn to, now that we have interrupted the flow, to Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting my learned colleague. However, I would like to object this line of questioning. Because for these important issues for this case, my learned colleague should invite and summon the person who gave this statement as a witness to testify before this Court and not cite his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Apostolski. Please carry on, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, later on, we see at 1100 hours on the same day the presence of the minister, Dr. Vlado Buckovski; the former chief of General Staff, General Pande Petrovski; and the defence minister's assistant for security and counter-intelligence, Colonel Kopacev, gave some information. So, were you following with me, Dr. Markovski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So we see that, on that weekend, General Stamboliski was both deputy chief of -- of the General Staff and the acting chief. We see that General Pande Petrovski remained present in the cabinet of the General Staff and continued to participate in meetings with the minister. On Tuesday, at pages 10741 to 10742 of the transcript, you explained that, during the crisis time, the General Staff had a functioning section called G3, which was the service for planning of operations. Now, going back to that last sentence of yours in paragraph 369: "It must be taken into account that the chief of the General Staff was changed on 10 August 2001. A new one had not been appointed and the preparations demanded a certain degree of planning." Are you still saying that, during that weekend, the General Staff of the army lacked sufficient competent personnel and expertise to plan an operation?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This does not refer to that, but it refers to the attitude of the president and Supreme Commander towards this activity; that is to say, there is an error in the statement by Stamboliski. With the decree, the president changed Pande Petrovski on the 10th of August, and we can see that he still remained in office. So there is this particular situation when the Supreme Commander, relieved of his duty, the Chief of Staff and the new one has not been appointed yet. The president and the Supreme Commander also communicate exclusively with the Chief of Staff according to the constitution and the Law on Defence and the Law on Service in the Army. At that time, it was just a handbook for service in the army. He decided to trust the preparation of this action in this particular manner as it is being described here. So it speaks about the relationship or of the president, the Supreme Commander, with the chief who is missing, or the deputy, who is not a chief yet; and this is how and why he has decided on acting on in manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovski --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Markovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski. Thank you. I apologise. We have an acting chief of the General Staff, and we had the chief who had been dismissed but remained at his post. So why couldn't the president simply use the General Staff in all of their planning capability?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff did not remain at his functional position, but he remained in the cabinet. When he was dismissed, he has no further function or responsibility or obligation that would belong to a Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters correction: Line 39:9, it should read that he was replaced on the "9th of August," and not the "10th of August."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. Should we take the first break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at five to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, if you could turn, please, to paragraph 334 of your report, please. In the start of paragraph 334, when you're talking about the events in Ljuboten, you say: "All of this points to the fact that an armed group of Albanian extremists was in the village of Ljuboten, that there were legitimate aims or purpose, and that there were armed provocations and incidents." Then, again, at the last few lines, you say: "The Macedonian security forces could and needed to undertake legitimate measures to eliminate the danger and threat to security." Have you been following with me?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm following.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, to paragraph 350; and, again, in that paragraph, you are still talking about the action in Ljuboten, and you say: "All this points to the fact that there were legitimate aims and armed provocations and incidents in the village of Ljuboten." Then, again, in the last sentence, you say: "The Macedonian security forces could and needed to undertake legitimate measures to eliminate the danger and threat to security." Again, if you turn to paragraph 387, it's actually the last paragraph of your report and that paragraph begins: "Proof of the legitimacy of the action by the security forces," et cetera. My question for you is this: If the Ljuboten action was legitimate, why would plans for the operations be kept secret from the authorities who were supposed to plan military actions; that is, the General Staff of the army of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I'm indicating that this is -- this was an idea of the president of the Republic of Macedonia and the Supreme Commander of the armed forces. For a long time, we discussed these notions here now, these days; and if memory serves, because the strain ask a bit too much for my small mind after these four days, I believe that, in the constitution, Article 89, paragraph 2 reads that the president is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Macedonia; and from this aspect, the president is not restricted by anything in the area of security and defence. So he could have done this. He is not even restricted by any law, any other regulation, to take over the command of this activity or another similar activity; although, there is a saying: The war is too serious a matter to be left to the Generals, and I would add to be left to the civilians to plan a war and think about it. So he is not restricted in any way. That was his assessment, his conclusion, and this is what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, if the Ljuboten action was legitimate and it involved the participation of police officers in a dangerous situation, why would the plans for the action be kept secret from the minister of internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, you misunderstood what I said. The president has the right, the president wanted to do that, the president can tell the minister of minister of the interior, "Stand aside and I am the were the and the Supreme Commander of the armed forces." There was one situation, and I have indicated in the report when the when the transformation of the bodies in Trebos were at stake. When the president told the minister of the interior, "Minister, I am the president of this state, and this is it," this is actually the right expression for the power that the constitution gives to the president of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But in the case of the action at Ljuboten, you don't have any specific information that the president told the minister of the interior to stand aside, do you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn back to paragraph 370, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the middle of paragraph 370, you say that a larger group of police officers entered the village of Ljubanci on the order of President Trajkovski. Then in footnote 229, you cite to a document that we looked at yesterday. It's Exhibit P303, the report from the 1st Guardist Brigade about the action and situation in the 3rd Guardist Battalion in the village of Ljuboten, dated 12 August 2001. Yesterday, at page 10824 of the transcript, we looked at this document, and we saw that this particular document does not demonstrate that the president gave a direct order to Major Despodov. I'd like to move on to another topic. Are you aware, Dr. Markovski, that there was fighting between the so-called NLA and the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia around Tetovo in early August 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, again, would not use the word "fighting" in the military sense, because the word "fighting" or "combat" is very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we use the term "armed violence"?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another video-clip, Dr. Markovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This will be 65 ter 1117.15. It has ERN number VOOO-7471, and it is clip 15. Again, this is a video material produced by Macedonian Radio and Television. It was produced on the 9th of August in 2001, and addresses the situation in Tetovo and the surrounding region. I may stop the clip at a very different intervals. If we could start it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Here we're seeing the village of Tetovo or the city of Tetovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: First of all, Dr. Markovski, we see an armoured personnel carrier going along the road here near Tetovo, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the highway, Skopje to Tetovo, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see an armoured personnel carrier. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is at 1.24 seconds of the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see, on the top of the armoured personnel carrier, we see an individual with a machine-gun mounted there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true. But I would like to ask you to repeat, once again, what was the date that this video was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: 9th August 2001.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the images of Tetovo do not correspond, this would be probably due to the editing. The images of Tetovo correspond to 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, all can I tell you is that this was produced on 9th August 2001 by Macedonian Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go back to this armoured personnel carrier, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not that I'm doubting that this is a feature aired on that day, but I want to say that those video-clip were made on the 24th of March, because I'm quite familiar with those, I'm not disputing that the APC has been videoed on the 9th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you're not the disputing that we see a machine-gun mounted on the top of that APC, are you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it is mounted. I see a human silhouette, and I see a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. By the way, this particular kind of armoured personnel carrier, is that what was called a Hermelin?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably now it, since you're asking it, and I will confirm this, in order to avoid having my authority under dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can just move forward a second, so that we can see this vehicle more close-up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the side of this vehicle, beneath the man with the machine-gun, we see the word "police." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue with this video-clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we stop the clip here, please. This is at 1 minute 52.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is the aftermath of the attack on the convoy of the army of the Republic of Macedonia at Karpalak. Are you familiar with this village -- with this footage.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this. This is the bus that was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So this footage was taken after the events at Karpalak, which occurred on the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue to go forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We're not getting any sound. Can we stop there, please. This is at 2 minutes and 26 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Here, we've just been informed by the journalist that: "In Tetovo, the streets are empty. Only passers by and those Tetovo residents who went out to buy food and the bare necessities can be noticed." Again, going back to this concept of a classic war or classic armed conflict in country X, we agreed before that in a classic armed conflict or a classic war, the daily life of civilians is often disrupted. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in crisis situations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so we understand what the gentleman said at the end, he said: "You can't defend Macedonia in Stip or in Strumnica." Those towns are much further to the south than Tetovo. Isn't that correct.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the eastern part of Macedonia and very far away from Tetovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this video-clip, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number P00609. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, because I think I always forget, if the transcript could also be part of that exhibit, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you for a moment about the event that occurred at Karpalak on the 8th of August, 2001, Dr. Markovski. The ten soldiers who died there, they were from Prilep, weren't they.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were from Prilep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after this incidence at Karpalak, there was violence in Prilep directed against property belonging to ethnic Albanians. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only against that, yes, that happened, violence was also directed against the barracks in Prilep, military barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would like to show another video-clip. I'm wondering if the quality of the sound could be improved somehow. This will be 65 ter 1120.2, and this is from Macedonian Radio and Television. It is -- was produced on the 8th of August, 2001, and it depicts some screens from Prilep. It was ERN number VOOO-7474, clip number 2. If we could start the video, please. I'm sorry, my colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting my learned friend but, I would like to ask you what is the relevance of this to the case, of this video-clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, part of the case is related to charges under Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. The Prosecution has specifically pleaded a joint criminal enterprise in this case, and it is the Prosecution's submission that the scenes we will see in this video from Prilep on the 8th of August will be relevant to the first and third theories of liability under joint criminal enterprise, particularly to the mens rea element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything further, Mr. Apostolski?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see what Prilep has to do with all of this; Prilep, which is 140 kilometres away from Skopje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could start this video-clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's not the right one. Hold on, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can stop there, please. This is the mosque in Prilep. This is at 28 seconds. We see that it is burning. Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see people standing in front of the mosque as it's burning at 1.15 and 1.16.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, did scenes like this that we just saw on this video broadcast on the news increase tensions in Macedonia at that time?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a reaction, a protest, expressing the protest because of the killing of the relatives, friends, fellow citizens. I don't know. This was a mass scale psychological situation. I don't see anything particular here that would make Prilep special, in the sense that this is something provided by divine intervention or something. This is a provoked reaction, a bit too harsh, and I do not justify it. But I believe that the video-clip is a by the partial. It depicts only facilities related to the ethnic Albanian population. Before I saw the clip, I told you that such protest was also expressed and demonstrated against the army, but actually in Prilep as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But broadcasting these kinds of images would likely increase tensions amongst the population in Macedonia at that time, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any TV situation follows its own programme and own plans. I don't see any legal obligation to prohibit the TV station from broadcasting this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this video-clip, please, and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P00610. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Back in August of 2001, the minister of Defence was Dr. Vlado Buckovski. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During one period, when the so-called broad coalition of the government of the Republic of Macedonia was in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question returns to August. Can we just focus on August for now. In August 2001, Buckovski was the minister of defence, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise then. Yes, you did say so. Please, this was just a lapse of concentration on my part because of the huge effort. Yes, yes. I apologise, once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during the events of the crisis in 2001, at least while he was the minister of defence, Dr. Buckovski was informed about the events that occurred, right, the security situation, the actions of the armed groups?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could guess with certainty, so it is more than a guess. Yes, the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Dr. Buckovski as well, in his role as -- in his position as minister of defence, he did his best to reduce fear and tension among the population. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are making me, again, to make assessments of my superiors. So, so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you give me a yes or a no to my question.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I said "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've told us previously, several times during your testimony, that, during 2001, the Republic of Macedonia was not in a state of war and it was not in a state of armed conflict. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I will confirm it again. The Republic of Macedonia, during 2001, was not in a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to show the witness another video-clip, please. This is 65 ter 1118.18. If we could please improve the quality of the sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is said to be the input signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't know what that means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From your equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, our equipment is the registry's equipment, so I don't know what we can exactly do about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two sources, the equipment or the video itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I have listened to the videos and I know that the sound is good, but I'll carry on. I'll carry on, Your Honours. 65 ter 1118.18 is a video-clip produced by MRTV, again, on the 9th of August, 2001. It has ERN number VOOO-7472; it's clip 18. We'll see here a statement of Vlado Buckovski about the events at Karpalak. If we could start it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We are now at 1 minute ran 5 of this video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what minister of defence Buckovski has just said is: "Let this great tragedy be the beginning of the end of the war, and not the beginning of a bloody civil war." So my question, Doctor, is if -- if this was not a war in Macedonia in August of 2001, why would Vlado Buckovski describe the situation as a war?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because he doesn't know precisely what a war situation means, or a state of war situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But he was the minister of defence at that time, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is like a provocation, the answer I provided. This is a verbal statement by the minister that you want to show as a qualification. Also, one might say that, back in 2001, I said that it was a war in one of my statements, but this is just a verbal statement that does not represent the constitutional and realistic situation in the Republic of Macedonia at that time. This verbal statement of his cannot be a corroboration that there was state of war in Macedonia. From all the documents that we reviewed and the factual situation that we reviewed in the Republic of Macedonia, in 2001, we did have a crisis, but not war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just to recall, earlier in your testimony, you explained --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
